title: Markov's and Chebyshev's Inequalities
short: For X ≥ 0, P(X ≥ a) ≤ E[X]/a; for any X with mean μ and standard deviation σ, P(|X − μ| ≥ kσ) ≤ 1/k².
trouble: Students read the bound as the exact probability, or use Markov's inequality for a variable that can be negative.

blocks.html: Often all we know about a random variable is its mean, or its mean and variance. That is still enough to say something definite about how likely large values are. The two inequalities here hold for every distribution, discrete or continuous, and they are the tools behind the law of large numbers.

Markov: if $X \ge 0$, then for every $a > 0$, $$P(X \ge a) \le \frac{E[X]}{a}.$$ Chebyshev: if $X$ has mean $\mu$ and standard deviation $\sigma$, then for every $c > 0$, $$P(\lvert X - \mu \rvert \ge c) \le \frac{\sigma^{2}}{c^{2}}, \quad \text{equivalently} \quad P(\lvert X - \mu \rvert \ge k\sigma) \le \frac{1}{k^{2}}.$$

Markov: compare two random variables. Wherever $X \ge a$, the quantity $a \cdot 1_{X \ge a}$ equals $a \le X$; elsewhere it is $0 \le X$, because $X \ge 0$. So $a \cdot 1_{X \ge a} \le X$ always, and taking expected values gives $a\,P(X \ge a) \le E[X]$.
Chebyshev: apply Markov to the nonnegative variable $(X - \mu)^{2}$ with $a = c^{2}$: $$P(\lvert X - \mu \rvert \ge c) = P\left((X - \mu)^{2} \ge c^{2}\right) \le \frac{E[(X - \mu)^{2}]}{c^{2}} = \frac{\sigma^{2}}{c^{2}}.$$

head: $k$
rows: Chebyshev: at least this much within $k\sigma$
blocks.cap: Chebyshev must hold for every distribution, so it is cautious.

blocks.title: Only the mean
blocks.q: Waiting times at a clinic average 10 minutes and are never negative. Bound the probability that a wait is at least 40 minutes.
steps: So at most a quarter of waits are that long, whatever the distribution.

blocks.title: Mean and spread
blocks.q: Test scores have mean 70 and standard deviation 5. Give a lower bound for the fraction of scores strictly between 60 and 80.
steps: 60 and 80 are $c = 10$ from the mean, which is $k = 2$ standard deviations.
$P(\lvert X - 70 \rvert \ge 10) \le \frac{25}{100} = \frac{1}{4}$, so at least $\frac{3}{4}$ of scores lie strictly between 60 and 80.

blocks.title: How tight is the bound?
blocks.q: For one fair die roll ($\mu = 3.5$, $\sigma^{2} = \frac{35}{12}$), compare Chebyshev's bound on $P(\lvert X - 3.5 \rvert \ge 2.5)$ with the true value.
steps: True value: only 1 and 6 are that far out, so $P = \frac{2}{6} = \frac{1}{3}$.
blocks.a: Bound $\frac{7}{15}$, true value $\frac{1}{3}$: correct, not tight.

blocks.html: Reading a bound as the exact probability ("Markov says the chance is $\frac{1}{4}$"), or using Markov's inequality for a variable that can be negative. If $X = \pm 10$ with equal chances, $E[X] = 0$, yet $P(X \ge 5) = \frac{1}{2}$, more than $\frac{0}{5}$. Check: Markov needs $X \ge 0$, and both inequalities give "at most" (or "at least") statements.
